text: Humayun came back 15 years later and took Delhi again.
A few months later, he slipped on the stairs of his library and died.
His son was 13 years old. His name was Akbar.
In 1556, at a second battle at Panipat, Akbar's army defeated the general Hemu.
and over the next 50 years Akbar built one of the richest empires on earth.
Akbar's secret weapon was not cannons, it was including people.
He met alliances with the Rajput kingdoms, many through marriage
and gave Rajput princes high posts in his army.
He scrapped the Jizya, a tax paid by non-Muslims
and his finance minister Raja Todarmal built a careful system for measuring land and setting taxes.
Akbar could barely read, yet he collected a huge library and had books read aloud to him every day.
At his new city, Fatehpur Sikri, he built a hall where Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian scholars debated religion in front of him.
Whispering, the debates got so heated, the Emperor had to play referee.
Not everyone accepted Akbar.
The Rajput ruler of Mewar, Maharana Pratap, refused to submit and fought Akbar's army
at Haldigati in 1576.
He kept resisting from the hills for the rest of his life.
Still, by the time Akbar died in 1605, the Mughal Empire was enormous and it was only
getting richer. Remember the hook? That quarter of the world's economy? That was
the India his grandson would rule. Checking his watch, excited. Now we are
getting to the cold!
